sections.body_md:
A vector \(d\) is a descent direction at \(x\) when the directional derivative is strictly negative. For a differentiable objective that derivative is the dot product of the gradient with \(d\). A negative value means the first-order model of \(f\) decreases as you leave \(x\) along \(d\). The model is enough to control a short step, even though a long step may later turn uphill.

Write the expansion \(f(x + t d) = f(x) + t\, \nabla f(x)^T d + o(t)\) as \(t\) tends to zero. Divide the change in \(f\) by the positive step. The remainder becomes negligible beside a fixed negative number, so the difference quotient stays negative for every sufficiently small \(t\). Multiplying back by that positive step shows that \(f\) itself drops.

The same dot product covers scaled directions. If \(D\) is symmetric positive definite and the gradient is not zero, the vector \(d = -D \nabla f(x)\) has directional derivative \(-\nabla f(x)^T D \nabla f(x)\). The quadratic form is positive, so the derivative is negative. Steepest descent is the case where \(D\) is the identity. A diagonal matrix with positive entries rescales the coordinates. A Newton direction uses the inverse Hessian when that inverse is positive definite. In every one of those cases the test is the same sign.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The test and the scaled construction are
\[
\nabla f(x)^T d < 0, \qquad d = -D \nabla f(x)
\]
with \(D\) symmetric positive definite. The directional derivative of that scaled direction is \(-\nabla f(x)^T D \nabla f(x)\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take the gradient \((5, -1)\) and the direction \((-3, 1)\). The dot product is \(5 \cdot (-3) + (-1) \cdot 1 = -15 - 1\).

The dock slope is -16. The sign is negative, so the direction is a descent direction, and a short enough step decreases \(f\). The negative gradient would have been \((-5, 1)\), a different vector. Its directional derivative is \(-(25 + 1) = -26\), also negative, and typically steeper. The number \(-16\) is only the test for the direction that was proposed.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
Reading a zero dot product as a descent direction is the usual slip. The definition asks for a strict inequality, and a zero derivative means the first-order model is flat. A second slip is to drop the minus sign in \(d = -D 
abla f\) and then still call the result a descent direction. Without the minus, the quadratic form \(
abla f^T D 
abla f\) is positive and the step climbs. A third is to demand the decrease for every positive step length. The first-order argument only controls a sufficiently short step. A fourth is to treat positive definiteness as optional. If \(D\) has a negative eigenvalue, \(-D 
abla f\) can point uphill for some gradients.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A descent iteration still has to choose the step length and a stopping test. The update is the current point plus a positive multiple of \(d\). On a quadratic the multiple that minimizes the objective along the line has a closed form. A sufficient-decrease test accepts a trial length without finding that exact minimizer. Both of those rules start from a direction that has already passed the sign test.
